newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Nike supervisor in Vietnam court for labour abuse.
newsitem.headline: Nike supervisor in Vietnam court for labour abuse.

text.p: The trial of a Taiwanese supervisor at a Nike Inc factory charged with physical abuse of workers opened in the southern Vietnam province of Dong Nai on Friday, a court official said.
Hsu Jiu Yen, if found guilty, would face a sentence ranging from a court reprimand to two years in jail, the official said.

Hsu is accused of forcing 56 of her workers at the Pou Chen Vietnam Enterprise Limited plant to jog twice around the two-km (1.2-mile) factory perimeter in the heat of the day for failing to wear regulation footwear.
According to local newspaper reports, 12 of the workers fainted and were taken to hospital.
Nike officials were not available to comment on the case.

The factory is one of five plants -- three South Korean and two Taiwanese -- producing shoes for the U.S. sportswear giant in Vietnam which were named last March by Vietnam Labour Watch for abuse of workers.

An independent review by former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Andrew Young, released earlier this week, found that workers at Nike factories in Asia were well-treated, but many were unaware of their rights and were often supervised by people who did not speak their language.

Young, who championed human rights while U.N. ambassador during the Carter administration, described the 12 factories he visited in China, Vietnam and Indonesia as "clean, organised, adequately ventilated and well-lit".

But he said confidential audits by an international firm found that religious holidays and days off were regularly denied to certain workers, workers on one shift were made to work overtime against their will and some workers were paid "training" or "probationary" wages beyond their actual training period.
